BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r1.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r1.claim: The heart is held in the prison of religious law and divine protection when it refuses worldly and lower-self prompting; even a prophet’s heart would incline without God’s protection.

BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r2.claim: ‘Then it appeared’ signals that the Aziz and his advisers changed their view about Joseph.

BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r3.claim: The signs they saw included the infant’s testimony and the torn shirt, among other evidence of Joseph’s innocence.

BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r4.claim: The courtiers’ stated aim was to silence public talk; the woman instead intended prison to humble Joseph and make people think him guilty.

BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r5.claim: Accounts give the imprisonment as five, seven, or, more famously, twelve years; Ibn al-Shaykh says the verse fixes no duration, only a long stay.

BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r6.claim: A period is linguistically indefinite and can be short or long; in juristic oaths an unqualified ‘while’ means six months unless a specific time was intended.

BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v4p163#2/r7.claim: The act of imprisonment is omitted and supplied by the next verse; the Aziz knew Joseph’s innocence, so the woman devised another tactic and accused him of disgracing her.

QASHANI:12:34-36/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:34-36/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:34-36/r2.claim: Joseph's imprisonment is spirit's retreat: spirit, soul, faculties, intellect, and thought agree to leave him in seclusion for spiritual vision, failed attraction, illusion's defeat, guidance, and thought's authority.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p343/r2.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p343/r2.speaker: عمر
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p343/r2.claim: ʿUmar reports hearing a reader say عتى حين, asks who taught him, then instructs Ibn Masʿūd to teach Quraysh Arabic rather than Hudhayl's dialect.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p343/r3.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p343/r3.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p343/r3.claim: The consonants in عتى and حتى can interchange because their articulation points are close; the more commonly used form is preferable, though the variant is permissible.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p323/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p323/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p323/r1.claim: Qatada says the signs were the women's hand wounds and the shirt torn from behind.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r5.claim: Badā means became apparent; Abū Ḥayyān prefers an understood subject referring to imprisonment, understood from the threat or the word sijn.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r6.claim: Grammarians and commentators usually posit an implicit subject explained by the context; another grammatical view makes the clause about imprisonment the subject, which Abū Ḥayyān rejects.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r7.claim: The pronoun in لهم refers to the ʿAzīz and his household; the signs are proofs of Joseph's innocence.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r8.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r8.claim: Mujāhid and others identify the shirt's tear as a sign; if the witness was an infant this was miraculous, while a grown witness would indicate innocence by ordinary inference.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r9.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says āyāt refers to clear evidence and its plural indicates several manifest proofs, perhaps including unmentioned evidence and the witness's statement.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r10.speaker: عكرمة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r10.claim: ʿIkrima's report that the signs included scratches on her face does not establish Joseph's innocence and is not a proof.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r11.speaker: السدي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r11.claim: Al-Suddī's report that the signs included cuts on the women's hands does not establish Joseph's innocence and is not a proof.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r12.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r12.claim: Layusjunannahu answers an unspoken oath within quoted speech; al-Ḥasan's tāʾ reading addresses the ʿAzīz or respectfully addresses his circle.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r13.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r13.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads with a tāʾ, addressing the ʿAzīz's circle or the ʿAzīz alone as a form of respect.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r14.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r14.speaker: ابن مسعود
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r14.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads ʿattā, replacing the ḥāʾ of ḥattā with ʿayn, a Hudhayl dialect; he was instructed to teach Quraysh usage instead.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r15.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r15.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r15.claim: Ḥīn denotes an unspecified time; any particular duration assigned here derives from Joseph's prison term, not the word's lexical meaning.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r16.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r16.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r16.claim: The proposed term in prison was a period in which they could see how Joseph behaved.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r17.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r17.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p273/r17.claim: The imprisonment illustrates women's plotting and a husband who yields authority to his wife despite her treachery and Joseph's innocence.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p274/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p274/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p274/r1.claim: A report says the ʿAzīz's wife told her husband that the Hebrew boy had defamed her, asking either to defend herself publicly or to be imprisoned as she was.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p274/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p274/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p274/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Joseph was carried on a donkey through Egyptian markets as a drum announced that he had sought his mistress and deserved prison.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p274/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p274/r3.speaker: أبو صالح
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p274/r3.claim: Abū Ṣāliḥ says Ibn ʿAbbās wept whenever he told this account.

FARRA:v2p43/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p43/r4.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p43/r4.claim: The signs of Joseph's innocence were that the shirt was torn from behind; the lām in ليَسجننه marks an oath or speech-like assertion, also used after الظن and العلم.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#2/r1.claim: Signs proving Joseph’s innocence include the torn shirt and women cutting their hands; Qatāda limits the signs to the shirt tear, treating the dual as plural. Mujāhid counts only the tear, since the cuts do not prove innocence.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#2/r2.claim: Some say the women’s cuts show Joseph’s beauty made them the likely initiators; others count his refusal of them as evidence of innocence because the ruler and advisers heard it. Ikrima reports Ibn ʿAbbās also named marks on Joseph’s body and a knife mark.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#2/r3.claim: Ikrima asked Ibn ʿAbbās about the signs; he listed the shirt tear, marks on Joseph’s body, and a knife mark. Other signs may have been omitted, as prophetic miracles often are.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#2/r4.claim: The subject of badā may be the verbal noun ‘decision,’ an opinion, or imprisonment understood from ‘they will imprison him’; the oath and response may be an object of implied saying or an explanatory clause.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#3/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#3/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#3/r1.claim: One view makes ‘they will surely imprison him’ the response to badā; another makes the full proposition its subject, as in 36:31 and 14:45, though most grammarians reject this.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#3/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#3/r2.speaker: المازني
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#3/r2.claim: Al-Māzinī selects the first subject analysis; Abū Ḥayyān selects the final one, where a pronoun refers to imprisonment understood from the sentence.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#3/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#3/r3.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#3/r3.claim: Abū Ḥayyān selects the final analysis of the subject of badā.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#3/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#3/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p236#3/r4.claim: The decision to imprison Joseph arose when his wife persuaded her husband, who yielded to her and entrusted his authority to her; a report says she framed Joseph as the offender and demanded his imprisonment.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p237/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p237/r1.speaker: الحسن
ALUSI-FULL:v12p237/r1.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads latasjunannahu as a direct address to the ruler or the ruler and advisers.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p237/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p237/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v12p237/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says ‘until a time’ means until city talk and rumors die down; the ruler’s apparent aim was temporary, while the wife wanted prison to humiliate Joseph and make people think him guilty.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p237/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p237/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p237/r3.claim: Reports give five, seven, or twelve years; al-Ālūsī avoids fixing a number and says only that the imprisonment was long. For most, ḥīn is an indefinite period, short or long.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p237/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p237/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
ALUSI-FULL:v12p237/r4.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reportedly read ʿattā with ʿayn, a Hudhayl dialect; ʿUmar wrote directing him to recite Quraysh’s ḥattā.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r3.claim: The Aziz and his associates first intended merely to order Joseph to be ignored, then decided to imprison him after seeing the signs of his innocence.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r4.claim: The signs included the torn shirt, the child’s speech, and the women cutting their hands and losing their senses.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r5.speaker: عطاء
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r5.claim: Ata says the prison term lasted until people stopped talking about the affair.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r6.speaker: عكرمة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r6.claim: Ikrima says Joseph remained imprisoned seven years.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r7.speaker: الكلبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r7.claim: Al-Kalbi says Joseph remained imprisoned five years.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r8.speaker: السدي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p239#2/r8.claim: Al-Suddi says the Aziz’s wife demanded either permission to leave and clear her name or Joseph’s imprisonment; God made prison a purification for Joseph from his desire for her.

NAHHAS:v2p329/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p329/r1.speaker: سيبويه
NAHHAS:v2p329/r1.claim: Sibawayh makes ليسجننه the subject of بدا; Muhammad ibn Yazid supplies a hidden noun, another reading means something new became known.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:35/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:35/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:35/r1.claim: After seeing evidence of Joseph's innocence—including the child's testimony, the torn shirt, the women's cutting their hands, and his resistance—the ruler's household decided to imprison him for a time.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:35/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:35/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:35/r2.claim: They imprisoned him either to see what would happen or to make people think he was the criminal; he remained in prison seven years.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:35/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:35/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:35/r3.claim: A reading has the feminine verb form, addressed by some people to the ruler honorifically or by the ruler to his attendants; 'atta is a Hudhayl dialect form.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r1.claim: Although the evidence should have kept Joseph from prison, God made imprisonment a means of frustrating the women's plot and establishing his rank, displaying divine power by overturning ordinary expectations.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r2.claim: The rulers knowingly chose an unjust and foolish imprisonment as part of God's overriding plan, which repeatedly overturns customary causes.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r3.claim: Bada means something appeared after being hidden and a change of opinion as a new consideration emerged; they decided to imprison him until the gossip faded.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r4.claim: One view says the period was seven years; another account says the wife told the governor that Joseph had disgraced her and asked either to leave and apologize or to join him in prison.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that Joseph was paraded on a donkey with a drum beaten before him, while callers in Egypt's markets announced his alleged crime and sentence.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r6.speaker: أبو صالح
BIQAI-FULL:v4p36#2/r6.claim: Abu Salih says Ibn Abbas wept whenever he related the story of Joseph's public humiliation.

DURR-FULL:v4p503/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p503/r6.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v4p503/r6.claim: After seeing signs—the torn shirt and the women's cut hands—the authorities decide to imprison Joseph for a time; the wife argues that he has disgraced her publicly.

DURR-FULL:v4p503/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p503/r7.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v4p503/r7.claim: The king jailed his baker for trying to poison him and jailed the cupbearer too, suspecting he had colluded in the poisoning.

DURR-FULL:v4p534/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas lists signs as the shirt's tear, marks on Joseph's body and knife marks; the wife urged prison lest people believe Joseph.

DURR-FULL:v4p534/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r2.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r2.claim: A second report identifies the signs as a tear in the shirt and scratches on the face.

DURR-FULL:v4p534/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r3.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r3.claim: Mujahid identifies the sign as the shirt torn from behind.

DURR-FULL:v4p534/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r4.speaker: ابن زيد
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r4.claim: Ibn Zayd says one of the signs was the speaking infant.

DURR-FULL:v4p534/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r5.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r5.claim: Qatadah identifies the signs as the women cutting their hands and the shirt's tear.

DURR-FULL:v4p534/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r6.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r6.claim: A discerning man advised the Aziz to imprison Joseph so people would excuse him and blame the household if he remained free to tell his story.

DURR-FULL:v4p534/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas describes three punishments for Joseph: prison over his desire, prolonged prison after asking the cupbearer to remember him, and the brothers' taunt that Benjamin had stolen as Joseph accused them of theft.

DURR-FULL:v4p534/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r8.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r8.claim: Ikrima says the prison sentence lasting until a time meant seven years.

DURR-FULL:v4p534/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r9.speaker: عمر
DURR-FULL:v4p534/r9.claim: Umar heard Ibn Masud's reading, then instructed him to teach the Quraysh dialect because the Qur'an was revealed in clear Quraysh Arabic, not Hudhayl.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r1.claim: The signs included the shirt's tear and knife marks; the wife warned that unless Joseph were imprisoned people would believe him.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r2.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r2.claim: The signs were the torn shirt and the women's scratched faces.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r3.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r3.claim: The wife told her husband the Hebrew servant had exposed her, and asked either to leave and defend herself or to have him imprisoned; the signs included the torn shirt and cut hands.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r4.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r4.claim: One of the signs was what the nursing woman said in the courtyard.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r5.speaker: ابن اسحاق
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r5.claim: The signs showed Joseph's innocence, including the shirt torn from behind.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r6.claim: Joseph was punished three times; the first punishment was imprisonment because of his desire for her.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r7.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2139#2/r7.claim: Gabriel told Joseph in prison that God called him righteous because grief, slavery, and imprisonment had not led him to obey his mistress in sin; God counted him among the purified and righteous.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r1.claim: The word “ḥīn” can mean morning or evening.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r2.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r2.claim: In a vow to cut off a boy's hand and imprison him for a period, the ruling was not to cut the hand and to imprison him for a year.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r3.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r3.claim: The word “ḥīn” can mean six months; Ṭāriq is reported to agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r4.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r4.claim: Another reported interpretation of “ḥīn” is seven years.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r5.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2140/r5.claim: For a vow to imprison a slave for a “ḥīn,” some periods can be fulfilled and others cannot; the unbounded period is the Qur'anic “until a time.”

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r1.claim: Then marks a surprising later turn: after Joseph's innocence became clear, the authorities decided to imprison him.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r2.claim: The chief wife feared gossip after the women dispersed, so she tried to cover Joseph's innocence by imprisoning him, making him appear guilty and perhaps returning him to her control.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r3.claim: “Them” refers to the chief wife's group of advisers and commanders.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r4.claim: The sentence with the oath lām is detached from “it appeared”; the omitted object can be inferred, showing suspension is not limited to verbs of thought, as Yunus ibn Habib held.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r5.speaker: يونس بن حبيب
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r5.claim: Yunus ibn Habib held that suspension is caused by an element with sentence-initial force and need not be limited to verbs of thought.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r6.claim: Grammarians differed over whether a clause may serve as a subject: Hisham and Tha'lab allowed it generally, while al-Farra and others allowed it with a cognitive verb and suspension; this verse is cited as evidence, though suspension fits better.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r7.claim: “Until a time” is indefinite; if spoken by the authorities, the term was open-ended, while if Qur'anic narration, its length is omitted because it is irrelevant to the story.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p267/r8.claim: The signs were proofs of Joseph's truth and the chief wife's falsehood.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r1.claim: After Joseph refused sin, the wife of al-Aziz allegedly told her husband that the Hebrew boy had publicly disgraced her and was explaining matters on his own terms; she demanded either release so she could defend herself and accuse him, or his imprisonment while she remained confined. They then chose prison.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says Joseph was put on a donkey, a drum was beaten, and he was announced through Egypt's markets as a Hebrew who desired his master and deserved prison; Abu Salih says Ibn Abbas wept whenever recounting it.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r3.claim: بدا means appeared, with a deleted subject estimated as بدو or رأي; the plural لهم refers to the king alone because the decision involved consultation, and ليسجننه is an oath clause.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r4.speaker: سيبويه
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r4.claim: Sibawayh's explicit position is that ليسجننه cannot be the grammatical subject of بدا, since a sentence cannot be its subject; the claim that it is the subject is wrong, and the sentence instead explains the omitted subject.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد وغيره
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r5.claim: Interpreters identify the signs as the torn shirt; Ikrima says Joseph's scratched face accompanied the shirt episode, and al-Suddi says the women cut their hands.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r6.claim: The point is that they decided on prison after signs had exonerated Joseph; scratched faces and cut hands do not prove innocence, whereas the shirt report does. If the speaker was an infant it was a great miracle; if an adult, the shirt offered an inference. 'Signs' may also mean whatever proofs were clear in degree.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p242#2/r7.claim: Alternatively, 'after they saw the signs' may mean that the overall circumstances showed Joseph was innocent, without identifying any one specific sign.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r1.claim: Ḥīn means an unspecified span of time, potentially short or long; the Qur’an uses it in both senses.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r2.speaker: عكرمة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r2.claim: He takes ḥīn here to mean seven years.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r3.claim: Another reported interpretation takes the period as one year; the author relates these durations to what was disclosed during Joseph’s imprisonment.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r4.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r4.claim: Umar heard a Hudhayli reading عتى حين and wrote Ibn Masud to teach people in Quraysh Arabic rather than Hudhayl’s dialect.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p243/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas counts three slips by Joseph: the episode with her, asking the cupbearer to remember him, and accusing the brothers of theft, which prompted the reply about Benjamin.

SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r1.claim: The subject of بدا is an implicit reference to the prison: the decision to imprison Joseph became apparent, supported by the readings of السجن.

SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r2.claim: A second parse makes the subject an implicit verbal noun from بدا, supported by the poet's explicit بداء.

SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r3.claim: Other analyses supply an implicit رأي from context or make the clause ليسجننه itself the subject, as the Kufans do.

SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r4.claim: حتى marks the endpoint of what precedes; the majority take ليسجننه as the response to an omitted oath contained within an implied statement.

SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r5.speaker: الحسن
SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r5.claim: Al-Hasan reads لتسجننه with address tāʾ, either as one person addressing another or as an honorific address to the chief.

SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r6.speaker: ابن مسعود
SAMIN-DURR:12:35/r6.claim: Ibn Masud reads عتى for حتى, replacing ḥāʾ with ʿayn; Umar directs him to teach Quraysh's dialect, and the author notes this substitution belongs to Hudhayl speech.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r1.speaker: أبو صالح عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r1.claim: One view says the signs leading to Joseph's imprisonment were the torn shirt and his cousin's judgment against the wife.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r2.speaker: مجاهد عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r2.claim: A second view includes the shirt being cut, the witness, the women's hand-cutting, and their awe at Joseph.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r3.speaker: الماوردي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r3.claim: Al-Mawardi says the signs were Joseph's beauty and chastity.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r4.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r4.claim: Wahb says the women urged the wife to imprison Joseph, hoping seclusion would let them entice him and stop public gossip that she hated him.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r5.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r5.claim: When Joseph remained unmoved, she later asked the master to imprison him because his presence exposed her; he agreed and treated him harshly.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r6.speaker: السدي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r6.claim: Al-Suddi reports that she demanded permission either to leave and clear herself or to jail Joseph as he had jailed her; the master and advisers chose imprisonment.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r7.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r7.claim: Al-Zajjaj says Aziz first ordered only that Joseph be ignored, then changed his mind.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r8.speaker: ابن الأنباري
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r8.claim: One reading of “then it appeared to them” is that imprisonment emerged as their plan through discussion and deliberation.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r9.speaker: ابن الأنباري
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r9.claim: Alternatively, they decided about Joseph that they must imprison him; the lām answers an unspoken oath.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r10.speaker: ابن عباس عن أبي صالح
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r10.claim: The otherwise unbounded word “a while” is estimated as five years in one report from Ibn Abbas.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r11.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r11.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas estimates one year.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r13.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r13.speaker: عطاء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r13.claim: Ata interprets the term as lasting until the gossip had died down.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r14.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r14.speaker: الماوردي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p221/r14.claim: Al-Mawardi says the term was unspecified; the author prefers this because the jailers set no fixed duration, while commentators estimated Joseph's actual stay.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p387/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p387/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p387/r1.claim: Though the authorities knew Yusuf was innocent, the proofs of his chastity made them judge temporary imprisonment expedient.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p387/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p387/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p387/r2.claim: Ibn Kathir conjectures that they imprisoned him to quiet public talk that could make it seem he had solicited her.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p387/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p387/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p387/r3.claim: When the king later summoned him, Yusuf refused release until his innocence was established and he could leave with his reputation clear.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p387/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p387/r4.speaker: السدي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p387/r4.claim: Al-Suddi says they jailed Yusuf so her conduct would not become public and expose her while clearing his reputation.

JISHUMI:v5p3637/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3637/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3637/r7.claim: Badw means appearing or becoming visible; badāʾ in opinion is a change of mind as new opinions appear.

JISHUMI:v5p3637/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3637/r8.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3637/r8.claim: The final nūn in ليكونا is emphatic and may be light or heavy; the nūn in ليسجنن is heavy, and pause forms differ from connected speech, as in لنسفعا.

JISHUMI:v5p3641/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3641/r1.speaker: عكرمة
JISHUMI:v5p3641/r1.claim: Until a time may mean seven years according to ʿIkrima, ten years according to al-Kalbī, or a long period according to al-Aṣamm.

JISHUMI:v5p3641/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3641/r2.speaker: أبو علي
JISHUMI:v5p3641/r2.claim: Other explanations say the imprisonment lasted until the rulers decided what to do, or until talk of the woman faded and Joseph was cut off from people.

JISHUMI:v5p3641/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3641/r6.speaker: الأصم
JISHUMI:v5p3641/r6.claim: Al-Aṣamm says the women imposed the apparent punishment of imprisonment but did not succeed in corrupting Joseph's religion.

JISHUMI:v5p3641/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3641/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3641/r7.claim: Their plotting and imprisonment were their own acts, not created by God.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r1.claim: The implicit subject of bada is a newly formed opinion, namely their decision to imprison Yusuf; the pronoun refers to the Aziz and his household.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r2.claim: The signs were evidence of Yusuf's innocence; the wife nevertheless persuaded and controlled her compliant husband, who followed her plan to imprison and humiliate him.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r3.claim: The wife either gave up hope that Yusuf would obey her or hoped prison would humble him and make him compliant.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r4.speaker: الحسن
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r4.claim: Al-Ḥasan's reading latasjunannahu addresses the Aziz and those around him, or addresses the Aziz alone deferentially.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r5.claim: Ḥattā ḥīn means for a period, apparently the duration the wife proposed while waiting to see what Yusuf would do.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r6.speaker: ابن مسعود
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r6.claim: Ibn Masʿud's reading ʿattā ḥīn is a Hudhayl dialect form.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r7.speaker: عمر
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p441/r7.claim: After hearing a man recite ʿattā ḥīn, ʿUmar asked his teacher and wrote Ibn Masʿud to teach Quraysh speech rather than Hudhayl speech.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p34#2/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p34#2/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p34#2/r1.claim: The signs they saw may be the torn shirt and the women's cut hands or Yusuf's evident chastity and beauty, which made them call him an angel rather than a human.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p34#2/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p34#2/r2.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p34#2/r2.claim: The term of imprisonment was six months according to Sa'id ibn Jubayr, seven years according to Ikrima, or an unspecified period according to many commentators.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p34#2/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p34#2/r3.speaker: السدي
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p34#2/r3.claim: Al-Suddi says al-Aziz's wife accused the Hebrew slave of slandering her and demanded either divorce so she could defend herself or that he be imprisoned as she had been; her husband jailed Yusuf.

MUJAHID:v1p315/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p315/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v1p315/r1.claim: Mujahid says the signs they saw included the torn back of Joseph's shirt.

MUQATIL:12:34-35/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:12:34-35/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:12:34-35/r2.claim: The torn shirt from behind proved Joseph innocent, but the husband imprisoned him after Zulaykha asked to keep him from approaching her.

MUQATIL:12:34-35/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:12:34-35/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:12:34-35/r3.claim: In prison Joseph comforted mourners, reassured the frightened, cared for the sick, and interpreted dreams; he described his lineage as a prophet through Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p188/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p188/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p188/r1.claim: The subject of 'it appeared to them' is implicit and supplied by the decision that they would imprison him; the pronoun refers to the minister and his household.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p188/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p188/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p188/r2.claim: The signs of Joseph's innocence included the shirt's tear, the women's cut hands, and the child's testimony.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p188/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p188/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p188/r3.claim: They imprisoned him to excuse the situation and silence gossip; the minister was compliant with his wife, who hoped prison would make Joseph submit, or feared public suspicion and accepted concealment instead of separation.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p188/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p188/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p188/r4.claim: The phrase 'until a time' leaves the period indefinite, as the wife apparently requested a period to see what would happen.

ZAJJAJ:v3p104/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p104/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p104/r1.claim: Badā is intransitive here with no expressed subject; Arabs say badā lī badāʾan when an opinion changes, usually omitting the noun because the context makes the change clear.

ZAJJAJ:v3p104/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p104/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p104/r2.claim: The decision was to imprison Joseph; the master had first ordered only that he be avoided, then changed his mind.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r1.claim: After seeing signs of Joseph's innocence, the Aziz and his advisers decided to imprison him to suppress the story and separate him from the woman; the alternative that the signs were blessings is less sound.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r2.speaker: مقاتل عن مجاهد عن ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r2.claim: The signs of innocence were the shirt, the witness, the women's cut hands, and their awe of Joseph.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r3.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r3.claim: Some say the woman, ashamed of people and despairing of having Joseph, accepted concealment in place of losing him, hoping to satiate her desire if denied his sight.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r4.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r4.claim: Another says she plotted to make Joseph tire of imprisonment and surrender himself.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r5.speaker: سيبويه
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r5.claim: Sibawayh treats يسجننه as the grammatical subject of بدا.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r6.speaker: المبرد
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r6.claim: Al-Mubarrad rejects a whole sentence as subject and says an implied verbal noun, بداء, is the subject, as in the cited poem's omitted حق.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r7.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r7.claim: Another parse supplies رأي and قالوا, with the oath-response lām in ليسجننه.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r8.speaker: أبو علي
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r8.claim: Abu Ali says the masculine verb reflects the masculine-dominant group of women and their male aides, indicated by لهم rather than لهن.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r9.speaker: السدي
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r9.claim: Al-Suddi says the wife caused Joseph's imprisonment by telling the Aziz that the Hebrew slave had disgraced her and asking that he be jailed.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r10.speaker: كثير من المفسرين
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r10.claim: Most commentators take حتى حين to mean an unspecified period.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r11.claim: Ibn Abbas says the imprisonment lasted until the talk in the city died down.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r12.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r12.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the period was six months.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r13.speaker: الكيا
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r13.claim: Al-Kiya reports a period of thirteen months.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r17.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r17.speaker: وهب
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35/r17.claim: Wahb says Joseph remained imprisoned twelve years.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r1.claim: The imprisonment purified Joseph from his desire for the woman; although the Aziz knew Joseph was innocent, he obeyed his wife and jailed him.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas counts three stumbles for Joseph: desiring the woman and being jailed, asking the cupbearer to remember him and remaining jailed, and accusing his brothers of theft.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r3.claim: Joseph was pressured by the threat of prison to commit adultery but refused; coercion by imprisonment does not permit adultery, by consensus.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r4.claim: Scholars differ over coercion by a severe beating; the sound view removes the sin of adultery alone, while the claim that its penalty remains is weak because God does not combine two torments, as 22:78 says.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:35#2/r5.claim: Joseph endured patiently and sought God's protection from the women's scheme, and God answered as described earlier.

RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r1.claim: After Joseph's innocence became evident, the wife falsely accused him of publicly defaming her and pressed her husband to choose between letting her leave to defend herself and imprisoning Joseph; the Aziz chose imprisonment to quiet scandal.

RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r2.claim: The signs of Joseph's innocence included the shirt torn from behind, scratches on her face, and the Aziz's judgment that her plot was great; other decisive signs were suppressed to hide the scandal.

RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r3.claim: Badā means that their opinion changed from what it had been before.

RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r4.claim: Grammarians reject making one verb the subject of another and therefore paraphrase the construction as then their imprisonment appeared advisable; al-Razi challenges the grammatical premise.

RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p106/r5.claim: He argues that a verb can be the subject of a statement: if the predicate says an item is a verb, either the verb itself is discussed or the alternative makes the statement false.

RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r1.claim: The continuation argues that if the subject in ضرب فعل is the verbal form, it is a noun and calling it a verb is false; if it is the verb, the example proves verbs can be discussed as subjects.

RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r2.speaker: أهل اللغة
RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r2.claim: Ḥīn is an unspecified span of time, either short or long.

RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the prison term as lasting until the talk and rumors about the scandal died away.

RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r4.claim: He reports estimates of five years, seven years, and twelve years from unnamed authorities and Muqatil; he says the exact duration is unknown but long, as 12:45 indicates.

ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.claim: Unlike Genesis' romantic account of Joseph's fortunes, the Qur'anic story illustrates God's unfathomable direction of human affairs: people may hate what is good for them or love what is bad for them.

ASAD-NOTES:12:34#n33/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:34#n33/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:34#n33/r1.claim: The phrase literally says that the idea occurred to them.

ASAD-NOTES:12:34#n34/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:34#n34/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:34#n34/r1.claim: Joseph was jailed to appease his master's wife, not because the master believed him guilty; Asad illustrates the husband's weakness through Zamakhshari's simile.

ASAD-NOTES:12:34#n34/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:34#n34/r2.speaker: Zamakhshari
ASAD-NOTES:12:34#n34/r2.claim: Zamakhshari likens the husband to a riding camel whose reins his wife held, illustrating his submission to her.

STUDYQURAN:12:intro/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:intro/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:12:intro/r10.claim: After false accusations and widespread rumors about the incident, Joseph is imprisoned.

STUDYQURAN:12:35/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:35/r1.speaker: Kl
STUDYQURAN:12:35/r1.claim: One interpretation takes them to mean Potiphar’s family and Zulaykhā.

STUDYQURAN:12:35/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:35/r2.speaker: Kl
STUDYQURAN:12:35/r2.claim: An alternative interpretation takes them to mean the members of Potiphar’s entourage whom he consulted.

STUDYQURAN:12:35/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:35/r3.speaker: JJ and Kl
STUDYQURAN:12:35/r3.claim: The signs were indications of Joseph’s innocence.

STUDYQURAN:12:35/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:35/r4.speaker: JJ
STUDYQURAN:12:35/r4.claim: Imprisonment was temporary, until rumors about Joseph and Zulaykhā subsided.

TAB-FULL:v13p147/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p147/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p147/r1.claim: The singular verb in 'it appeared to them' refers to the Aziz, who is not named or individually specified; al-Tabari compares the construction with a report where one person speaks as 'the people.'

TAB-FULL:v13p147/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p147/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p147/r2.claim: After seeing signs of Yusuf's innocence, they reversed their apparent decision to release him and decided to imprison him; the signs included the rear shirt tear, scratches on the face, and women's cut hands.

TAB-FULL:v13p147/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p147/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v13p147/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the signs as the tear in Yusuf's shirt and scratches on the woman's face.

TAB-FULL:v13p147/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p147/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v13p147/r4.claim: Mujahid identifies the sign as the tear in Yusuf's shirt from behind.

TAB-FULL:v13p147/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p147/r5.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v13p147/r5.claim: Qatada says the signs were the women's hand wounds and the tear in Yusuf's shirt.

TAB-FULL:v13p147/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p147/r6.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v13p147/r6.claim: Al-Suddi lists the shirt and the women's cut hands among the signs.

TAB-FULL:v13p150/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r1.claim: They intended to keep Yusuf imprisoned until they chose their next course; al-Tabari says God made this confinement a punishment for Yusuf's prior inclination toward the woman and an expiation.

TAB-FULL:v13p150/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas relates three lapses: Yusuf's inclination led to prison, asking the cupbearer for help prolonged it, and his brothers' accusation of theft led to a brother's accusation against him.

TAB-FULL:v13p150/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r3.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r3.claim: Al-Suddi says the Aziz's wife asked her husband either to let her leave and explain herself or imprison Yusuf because he was telling people she had solicited him.

TAB-FULL:v13p150/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r4.speaker: أهل العربية من البصرة
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r4.claim: One Basran grammatical explanation says the emphatic lām and nūn in la-yasjununnahu occur where an interrogative construction with ay would otherwise appear.

TAB-FULL:v13p150/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r5.speaker: بعض أهل العربية
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r5.claim: Some grammarians reject the interrogative explanation: the lām is an oath, since an emphatic nūn does not follow a question such as 'will you stand?'.

TAB-FULL:v13p150/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r6.speaker: نحوي من الكوفة
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r6.claim: A Kufan grammarian says bada lahum carries the sense of 'they said/decided,' and speech can introduce either an oath or an interrogative, licensing the construction.

TAB-FULL:v13p150/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r7.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v13p150/r7.claim: Ikrima interprets the time until which Yusuf was imprisoned as seven years.

TABATABAI:12:33-34/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34/r7.claim: Some took the response as granting a prayer for imprisonment, but the author rejects this: the later wording says only then did they decide to imprison him.

TABATABAI:12:33#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33#2/r1.speaker: علي بن الحسين
TABATABAI:12:33#2/r1.claim: A report from Imam al-Sajjād recounts Joseph’s resistance to the wife, the child’s shirt test, the women’s gathering and private approaches, Joseph’s plea for protection, and his eventual imprisonment.

TABATABAI:12:35/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:35/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:35/r1.claim: The imprisonment begins a period of several years that brings Joseph close to the king and to Egypt’s authority; in prison he calls people to monotheism and first identifies his Abrahamic family.

TABATABAI:12:35/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:35/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:35/r2.claim: Badā means that a new opinion appeared after it had not existed; ‘they’ refers to the master, his wife, and their circle of advisers and attendants.

TABATABAI:12:35/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:35/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:35/r3.claim: The signs of Joseph’s innocence include the child’s testimony, his shirt torn from behind, the pair racing to the door, and perhaps the women’s amazement and the wife’s admission.

TABATABAI:12:35/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:35/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:35/r4.claim: The lām is an oath of firm resolve; ‘until a time’ means until the public story of the seduction subsides and people forget it.

TABATABAI:12:35/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:35/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:35/r5.claim: One possible motive was protecting the master’s household from shame and preventing public disorder or women’s infatuation with Joseph’s extraordinary beauty.

TABATABAI:12:35/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:35/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:35/r6.claim: Later evidence shows the wife may have misled her husband into doubting Joseph’s innocence; she may have arranged or ordered prison both to protect herself and to punish him into obedience.

TABATABAI:12:41-42#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:41-42#2/r1.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
TABATABAI:12:41-42#2/r1.claim: In the al-Qummi report through Abu al-Jarud, the signs preceding Joseph’s imprisonment were the child’s testimony, the shirt torn from behind, and the pair racing to the door while struggling.

TABRISI:12:34-35/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:34-35/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:34-35/r2.claim: Although the women were previously mentioned, the masculine plural 'them' refers to the king; another reading takes it as Zuleikha and her helpers, with masculine agreement for a mixed group.

TABRISI:12:34-35/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:34-35/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:34-35/r3.claim: The signs proving Yusuf's innocence were the shirt torn from behind and the women's cut hands, according to Qatada and others.

TABRISI:12:34-35/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:34-35/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:34-35/r4.claim: Another interpretation takes the signs as evidence that the women had despaired of obtaining Yusuf.

TABRISI:12:34-35/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:34-35/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:34-35/r5.claim: The grammatical subject of بدا is omitted and understood as بداء; the decision that appeared was the decision to imprison him.

TABRISI:12:34-35/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:34-35/r6.speaker: السدي
TABRISI:12:34-35/r6.claim: Al-Suddi says Zuleikha told her husband that Yusuf had publicly disgraced her by saying she had seduced him, and demanded release to explain herself or his imprisonment.

TABRISI:12:34-35/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:34-35/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:34-35/r7.claim: One explanation says they imprisoned Yusuf so the public would assume he was guilty, since criminals are the ones imprisoned.

TABRISI:12:34-35/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:34-35/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:34-35/r8.claim: Another explanation is that the prison was near Zuleikha, who wanted to see Yusuf when she looked out.

TABRISI:12:34-35/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:34-35/r9.speaker: عكرمة، الكلبي، الجبائي
TABRISI:12:34-35/r9.claim: The imprisonment lasted seven years according to ʿIkrima, five according to al-Kalbi, or until the affair was forgotten and Yusuf's news faded according to al-Jubbaʾi.

THALABI:v5p220/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p220/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p220/r3.claim: The officials who saw signs of Joseph’s innocence nevertheless decided to imprison him for a time.

THALABI:v5p220/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p220/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p220/r4.claim: The signs of innocence included the shirt torn from behind, scratches to the face, and the women cutting their hands.

THALABI:v5p220/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p220/r5.speaker: الفراء
THALABI:v5p220/r5.claim: Al-Farra says the lām in the oath and in reported present-tense speech is used because both expressions carry the sense of speech and oath.

THALABI:v5p220/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p220/r6.speaker: عكرمة
THALABI:v5p220/r6.claim: Ikrima says the phrase until a time means nine years.

THALABI:v5p220/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p220/r7.speaker: الكلبي
THALABI:v5p220/r7.claim: Al-Kalbi says Joseph remained imprisoned five years.

THALABI:v5p220/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p220/r8.speaker: السدي
THALABI:v5p220/r8.claim: Al-Suddi says the wife complained Joseph had publicly accused her of seducing him and asked either to leave to defend herself or for him to be imprisoned too.

THALABI:v5p220/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p220/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p220/r9.claim: God made prison a purification for Joseph’s desire toward the woman and an expiation for his lapse.

THALABI:v5p220/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p220/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v5p220/r10.claim: Ibn Abbas counts three lapses by Joseph: the episode leading to prison, asking the cupbearer to remember him, and accusing his brothers of theft.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r1.speaker: وهب
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r1.claim: Zulaykhā complained that Joseph had disgraced her publicly and asked to leave to defend herself or have him jailed as she had been; the governor and his associates decided to imprison him.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r2.speaker: السدي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r2.claim: Al-Suddī shares the report that Zulaykhā demanded Joseph be jailed because he had exposed her.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r3.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r3.claim: The signs of Joseph's innocence were the shirt torn from behind, the scratched face, and the sage's ruling against her, including her admission that it was the women's plot.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r4.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r4.claim: Qatāda includes the women's cutting their hands among the signs; al-Wāḥidī questions how that demonstrates Joseph's innocence.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r5.claim: One grammatical analysis supplies a hidden subject for بدا, indicated by ليسجننه; the oath-lām in that verb answers an unstated oath, and its third-person form follows the unseen subject.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r6.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r6.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says ليسجننه itself fills the subject position of بدا: the idea is that their decision to imprison him appeared, with the oath-lām standing for a quotation.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r7.speaker: أبو عثمان
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r7.claim: As transmitted by Abū ʿAlī, Abū ʿUthmān supplies an implicit subject such as بدو; the noun can serve as subject because بدو means an opinion appeared.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r8.speaker: أبو عثمان
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p108#2/r8.claim: Abū ʿUthmān alternatively treats ليسجننه as quoted speech after an omitted أمر قالوا, like the omitted قالوا before “we worship them” in 39:3.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r1.speaker: أهل اللغة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r1.claim: A ḥīn is an unspecified period of time that can be short or long.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r2.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ's report, the imprisonment lasted until the gossip and scandal in the city died down.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r3.claim: In al-Kalbī's report, the period was five years.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r4.speaker: سفيان
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r4.claim: Sufyān and ʿIkrima say Joseph was imprisoned for seven years.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r5.speaker: عكرمة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r5.claim: ʿIkrima agrees with Sufyān that the period was seven years.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r6.speaker: مقاتل بن سليمان
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r6.claim: Muqātil b. Sulaymān says Joseph remained imprisoned for twelve years.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r7.claim: The governor agreed to his wife's request and imprisoned Joseph despite knowing he was innocent.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r8.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r8.claim: The commentators say God made the imprisonment a purification for Joseph from his desire for the woman and an expiation for his lapse.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r9.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p110/r9.claim: God left the period unspecified to honor scholars and direct people to them to solve interpretive difficulties.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:34-36/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:34-36/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:34-36/r2.claim: After seeing signs of Joseph's innocence, the ruler and his companions decided to imprison him until the public blame stopped.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:34-36/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:34-36/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:34-36/r3.claim: The ruler's wife said Joseph had exposed her by telling people she had tried to seduce him, so she wanted him imprisoned until gossip ended.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:35/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:35/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:35/r1.claim: Aziz’s household sought to protect its reputation and conceal the affair; the woman wanted to punish Joseph’s disobedience by blaming the slave and imprisoning him.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:35/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:35/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:35/r2.claim: Despite evidence that Joseph was innocent and the woman guilty, Aziz and his associates chose to imprison him for a time.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Joseph’s imprisonment begins another trial: his powerful hosts knew the reality but judged a short prison term would silence gossip and lessen Zelicha’s infatuation by keeping him away.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The signs are evidence that Joseph was innocent.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Aziz and his relatives knew Joseph was blameless and Zelicha was entirely at fault.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: To avoid embarrassment, they proposed imprisoning Joseph for a while.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: They expected Zelicha's infatuation and public interest to fade, leaving people to think Joseph was guilty and punished.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Masters had unrestricted power over enslaved people, so Aziz could readily send Joseph to prison.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Aziz's government office and rank in the royal guard would have let him overcome any obstacle to imprisonment.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: This begins another trial; although people might deem it the hardest, Joseph desired it because faith and character mattered most.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p234/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p234/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p234/r1.claim: The opening lexical notes define trade, entreaty as gentle request, seeking marriage, locking, tearing cloth, master or chief, and imprisonment.

AKHFASH:v1p397/r3.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p397/r3.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p397/r3.claim: The emphatic nūn in ليسجننه is licensed because the clause can host an interrogative, as in asking which of them will take someone.
